title: Kedgeree
subtitle: Smoked haddock and spiced rice with boiled eggs and butter
excerpt: Kedgeree is a British-Indian breakfast dish that became a staple of the Victorian and Edwardian grand breakfast table: flaked smoked haddock folded into buttered rice with mild spices, hard-boiled eggs, and parsley. It is a generous, warming dish that works as well for brunch as for supper.
sourceNotes: Kedgeree derives from the Indian dish khichri, a simple rice and lentil preparation brought back to Britain by returning colonial servants and adapted with smoked haddock in the nineteenth century. The British version replaced the lentils with fish and added eggs, cream, and curry powder.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Poach the fish a day ahead. Cook the rice fresh and combine on the day.

glossaryTerms.definition: A British-Indian breakfast dish of smoked haddock, spiced rice, and hard-boiled eggs. Derived from the Indian khichri and popularised during the British colonial period.

content.text: is a forgiving dish: the ratios are flexible, the spices are gentle, and the smoked haddock does most of the flavour work. The rice is cooked separately, the fish is poached in milk, and the two come together in a buttered pan with spices at the end. Make sure the rice is cooked dry (not wet and steaming) before adding the fish.
Poach the fish and cook the eggs

Put the smoked haddock in a pan and pour over {{whole-milk}} of milk. Bring to a gentle simmer and poach for 6 to 8 minutes until the fish flakes easily. Lift out, remove the skin, and flake into large pieces. Discard the poaching milk or reserve for another use.
Hard-boil {{eggs}} eggs in simmering water for 9 minutes. Cool in cold water, peel, and quarter.
Cook {{basmati-rice}} of basmati rice according to packet instructions. Drain and spread on a tray to cool and dry for 5 minutes.

Melt {{unsalted-butter}} of butter in a large pan over medium heat. Add {{onion}} sliced onion and cook for 8 minutes until soft and golden. Add {{curry-powder}} of curry powder and {{turmeric}} of turmeric; cook for 1 minute. Stir in the cooked rice and fold through the flaked fish gently, keeping the pieces large. Add the cream if using. Season carefully, the fish is already salty.
Serve in warm bowls, topped with the quartered eggs and chopped parsley, with lemon wedges alongside.

items.symptom: The rice has turned to mush when combined with the fish
items.cause: The rice was too wet, or it was stirred too vigorously.
items.fix: Drain the rice thoroughly and spread it to steam-dry before combining. Fold gently rather than stirring.

items.cause: Smoked haddock is already heavily salted and the poaching milk adds more.
items.fix: Do not add salt until the dish is almost finished. Taste after combining the fish and rice before seasoning.

items.symptom: The hard-boiled eggs have grey rings around the yolks
items.fix: 9 minutes in simmering water, then immediately into cold water. The cold water stops the cooking and prevents the iron-sulphur reaction that causes the grey ring.

items.symptom: The curry flavour is too dominant
items.cause: Too much curry powder was used, or the powder was very fresh and potent.
items.fix: Use 1 tablespoon of mild curry powder as a starting point. The spice should be present but not overwhelming , kedgeree is a subtle dish.

content.text: Kedgeree is one of the most enduring examples of British-Indian cooking. It was carried back from the subcontinent, adapted with smoked fish, and became a fixture of the Victorian breakfast table. It fell from fashion in the mid-twentieth century but has come back as a weekend brunch dish. Its mild warmth and ease of making suit a slow morning very well.
